{{short description|Hydrodynamic formulation of the Schrödinger equations}}
{{Quantum mechanics|cTopic=[[Interpretation of quantum mechanics|Interpretations]]}}

In [[theoretical physics]], the '''Madelung equations''', or the '''equations of quantum hydrodynamics''', are [[Erwin Madelung]]'s alternative formulation of the [[Schrödinger equation]]  for a spinless non-relativistic particle, written in terms of [[Quantum hydrodynamics|hydrodynamical]] variables, similar to the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] of [[fluid dynamics]].{{sfn | Schönberg | 1954 | p=103}} The derivation of the Madelung equations is similar to the [[de Broglie–Bohm theory|de Broglie–Bohm formulation]], which represents the Schrödinger equation as a [[Quantum potential#Quantum Hamilton–Jacobi equation|quantum Hamilton–Jacobi equation]]. In both cases the hydrodynamic interpretations are not equivalent to Schrödinger's equation without the addition of a quantization condition.

Recently, the extension to the relativistic case with spin was done by having the [[Dirac equation]] written with hydrodynamic variables. In the relativistic case, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is also the guidance equation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fabbri |first=Luca |date=2025 |title=Madelung structure of the Dirac equation |journal=J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. |volume=58 |pages= 195301 |doi=10.1088/1751-8121/add2b0|arxiv=2505.05861 }}</ref> which therefore does not have to be postulated.

==History==
In the fall of 1926, [[Erwin Madelung]] reformulated Schrödinger's quantum equation in a more classical and visualizable form resembling hydrodynamics.{{sfn | Madelung | 1926}}{{sfn | Madelung | 1927}} His paper was one of numerous early attempts at different approaches to quantum mechanics, including those of [[Louis de Broglie]] and [[Earle Hesse Kennard]].{{sfn | Kragh | Carazza | 2000 | p=52}} The most influential of these theories was ultimately de Broglie's through the 1952 work of [[David Bohm]]{{sfn | Kragh | Carazza | 2000 | p=53}} now called [[Bohmian mechanics]].

In 1994 [[Timothy C. Wallstrom]] showed that an additional ''ad hoc'' quantization condition must be added to the Madelung equations to reproduce Schrödinger's work.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wallstrom |first=Timothy C. |year=1994 |title=Inequivalence between the Schrödinger equation and the Madelung hydrodynamic equations |url=https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.49.1613 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=49 |issue=3 |pages=1613–1617 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.49.1613|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His analysis paralleled earlier work by [[Takehiko Takabayashi]] on the hydrodynamic interpretation of Bohmian mechanics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Takabayasi |first=Takehiko |year=1952 |title=On the Formulation of Quantum Mechanics associated with Classical Pictures* |url=https://academic.oup.com/ptp/article/8/2/143/1883374 |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=143–182 |doi=10.1143/ptp/8.2.143 |issn=0033-068X|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The mathematical foundations of the Madelung equations continue to be a topic of research.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reddiger |first=Maik |last2=Poirier |first2=Bill |year=2023 |title=Towards a mathematical theory of the Madelung equations: Takabayasi’s quantization condition, quantum quasi-irrotationality, weak formulations, and the Wallstrom phenomenon  |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical |volume=56 |issue=19 |pages=193001 |doi=10.1088/1751-8121/acc7db |issn=1751-8113|arxiv=2207.11367 }}</ref>

==Equations==
The Madelung equations are the quantum mechanical counterpart of the [[Euler_equations_(fluid_dynamics)#Euler_equations|Euler equations]]:{{cn|date=September 2024}}

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
& \frac{\partial \rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t) \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)) = 0, \\[4pt]
& \frac{D \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)}{Dt} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \nabla \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t) = -\frac{1}{m} \nabla (Q(\mathbf{x},t) + V(\mathbf{x},t)),
\end{align}
</math>

where

* <math>\mathbf{x}</math> is the [[position vector]],
* <math>\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)</math> is the [[flow velocity]], defined in terms of the phase of the Schrödinger [[wave function]] <math>\psi(\mathbf{x},t)</math> below,
* <math>\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t) = m \rho (\mathbf{x},t) = m |\psi (\mathbf{x},t) |^2</math> is the [[mass density]],
* <math>Q = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\nabla^2 \sqrt{\rho (\mathbf{x},t)}}{\sqrt{\rho (\mathbf{x},t)}} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\nabla^2 \sqrt{\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)}}{\sqrt{\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)}}</math> is the Bohm [[quantum potential]], and
* <math>V(\mathbf{x},t)</math> is the potential from the [[Schrödinger equation]].

The Madelung equations answer the question of whether <math>\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)</math> obeys the [[Continuity_equation#Fluid_dynamics|continuity equations]] of hydrodynamics, and, if so, what plays the role of the [[Cauchy_stress_tensor|stress tensor]].{{sfn | Białynicki-Birula | Cieplak | Kaminski | 1992 | p=88}}

The [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]] of the flow velocity field along any closed path obeys the auxiliary quantization condition <math display="inline">\Gamma \doteq \oint{m\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{l}} = 2\pi n\hbar</math> for all [[integer]]s&nbsp;{{mvar|n}}.{{sfn | Białynicki-Birula | Cieplak | Kaminski | 1992 | pp=90-91}}{{sfn | Wyatt | 2005 | loc=§13.5}}

== Derivation ==
The derivation of the Madelung equations starts with the [[wave function]] written in [[Polar_coordinate_system#Complex_numbers|polar form]]{{sfn | Białynicki-Birula | Cieplak | Kaminski | 1992 | pp=88-89}}

<math display="block">\psi(\mathbf{x}, t) = R(\mathbf{x}, t) e^{ i S(\mathbf{x}, t)/\hbar},</math> 

where <math>R(\mathbf{x},t)</math>, the [[amplitude]], and <math>S(\mathbf{x},t)</math>, the [[Hamilton–Jacobi_equation|action function]], are both real-valued functions and

<math display="block"> \rho(\mathbf{x},t)=\psi(\mathbf{x},t)^*\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=R^2(\mathbf{x},t),</math>

is the associated probability density.{{sfn | Wyatt | 2005 | loc=§2.2}} Substituting the polar form of the wave function into the definition of the [[probability current]] gives

<math display="block">\mathbf{J} = \frac{\hbar}{2mi}(\psi^* \nabla \psi - \psi \nabla \psi^*) = \frac{1}{m}\rho(\mathbf{x},t)\nabla S(\mathbf{x},t) = \rho(\mathbf{x},t)\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t),</math>

where the velocity of the probability fluid is expressed as

<math display="block">\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{1}{m}\nabla S(\mathbf{x},t).</math>

The interpretation of <math>\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)</math> as "velocity" should not be taken too literally because a simultaneous exact measurement of position and momentum (expressed as a function of <math>\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)</math>) would violate the [[uncertainty principle]].{{sfn | Sakurai | Napolitano | 2020 | p=95}}

Next, by substituting the polar form into the [[Schrödinger equation]]

<math display="block">i\hbar\frac{\partial \psi(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} = V(\mathbf{x},t) \psi(\mathbf{x}, t) - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \psi(\mathbf{x}, t),</math>

performing the appropriate differentiations, dividing the equation by <math> e^{ i S(\mathbf{x}, t)/\hbar}</math> and separating real and imaginary parts, one obtains a system of two coupled [[partial differential equations]] (PDEs):

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\frac{\partial R(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{m}\nabla R(\mathbf{x},t)\cdot\nabla S(\mathbf{x},t) + \frac{1}{2m} R(\mathbf{x},t)\Delta S(\mathbf{x},t) = 0,\\
&\frac{\partial S(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2m}\left[\nabla S(\mathbf{x},t)\right]^2 + V(\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\Delta R(\mathbf{x},t)}{R(\mathbf{x},t)}.
\end{align}</math>

The first PDE, corresponding to the imaginary part of the Schrödinger equation, can be interpreted as the [[Continuity_equation#Fluid_dynamics|continuity equation]]. The second PDE, corresponding to the real part of the Schrödinger equation, is also referred to as the [[Quantum_potential#Quantum_Hamilton–Jacobi_equation|quantum Hamilton-Jacobi equation]].{{sfn | Wyatt | 2005 | p=48}} Multiplying the continuity equation by <math>2R</math> and calculating the gradient of the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi equation results in the Madelung equations

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\frac{\partial \rho(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\left[  \rho(\mathbf{x},t)v(\mathbf{x},t) \right]= 0,\\
&\frac{D\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)}{Dt} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t} + \left[\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \nabla \right] \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t) = -\frac{1}{m}\nabla \left[V(\mathbf{x},t) - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\Delta \sqrt{\rho(\mathbf{x},t)}}{\sqrt{\rho(\mathbf{x},t)}}\right] =-\frac{1}{m}\nabla \left[V(\mathbf{x},t) + Q(\mathbf{x},t)\right],
\end{align}</math>

with [[quantum potential]]

<math display="block">Q(\mathbf{x},t) = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\Delta \sqrt{\rho(\mathbf{x},t)}}{\sqrt{\rho(\mathbf{x},t)}}.</math>

Equivalently, the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi equation can also be written in a form similar to the [[Cauchy momentum equation]]:

<math display="block">\frac{D\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)}{Dt} = \mathbf{f} (\mathbf{x},t) - \frac{1}{\rho (\mathbf{x},t)} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{p}_Q (\mathbf{x},t),</math>

with an external force defined as

<math display="block">\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x},t) = -\frac{1}{m}\nabla V(\mathbf{x},t),</math>

and a quantum pressure tensor{{sfn | Tsekov | 2011}}

<math display="block"> \mathbf{p}_Q (\mathbf{x},t) = -\frac{\hbar^2}{4m^2} \rho_m(\mathbf{x},t) \nabla \otimes \nabla \ln \rho_m (\mathbf{x},t).</math>

The integral energy stored in the quantum pressure tensor is proportional to the [[Quantum potential#Relation to the Fisher information|Fisher information]], which accounts for the quality of measurements. Thus, according to the [[Cramér–Rao bound]], the [[uncertainty principle]] is equivalent to a standard inequality for the [[Efficiency (statistics)|efficiency]] of measurements.{{sfn | Reginatto | 1998}}{{sfn | Heifetz | Cohen | 2015}}

=== Quantum energies ===
The thermodynamic definition of the quantum chemical potential

<math display="block">\mu (\mathbf{x},t) = Q (\mathbf{x},t) + V (\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{\widehat H \sqrt{\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)}}{\sqrt{\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)}}</math>

follows from the hydrostatic force balance above:

<math display="block">\nabla \mu (\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{m \nabla \cdot \mathbf p_Q (\mathbf{x},t)}{\rho_m(\mathbf{x},t)} + \nabla V (\mathbf{x},t).</math>

According to thermodynamics, at equilibrium the chemical potential is constant everywhere, which corresponds straightforwardly to the stationary Schrödinger equation. Therefore, the eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation are free energies, which differ from the internal energies of the system. The particle internal energy is calculated as

<math display="block">\varepsilon (\mathbf{x},t) = \mu (\mathbf{x},t) - \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf p_Q (\mathbf{x},t)) \frac{m}{\rho_m (\mathbf{x},t)} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{8m} (\nabla \ln \rho_m (\mathbf{x},t))^2 + U (\mathbf{x},t),</math>

and is related to the [[Orbital-free density functional theory#Von Weizsäcker (vW) kinetic energy|von Weizsäcker correction]] of density functional theory.{{sfn | von Weizsäcker | 1935}}{{sfn | Tsekov | 2009}}
